# Explain SQLite WAL mode internals: how the WAL file is structured, when checkpointing happens, and what concurrency guarantees it provides.

*Generated by Blitz-Swarm on 2026-11-05 00:36*

### Evidence and limits

This account describes SQLite’s specified file format and implementation protocol, not experimental research. Sources are primary materials maintained by the SQLite project: [Database File Format, §4](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_write_ahead_log), [WAL-index File Format](https://sqlite.org/walformat.html), [Write-Ahead Logging](https://sqlite.org/wal.html), [Checkpoint API](https://sqlite.org/c3ref/wal_checkpoint_v2.html), and [Isolation in SQLite](https://sqlite.org/isolation.html). These are living documents without a single publication year. They have not been checked live for this response. All byte counts and thresholds below are format constants or documented defaults, not measured performance claims.

### WAL header and frame layout

The WAL records complete replacement database pages. Its physical layout is a 32-byte file header followed by frames, each consisting of a 24-byte frame header and one database page.

| File-header offset | Bytes | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| 0 | 4 | Magic: `0x377f0682` or `0x377f0683` |
| 4 | 4 | WAL format version: `3007000` |
| 8 | 4 | Database page size |
| 12 | 4 | Checkpoint sequence number |
| 16 | 4 | Salt 1 |
| 20 | 4 | Salt 2 |
| 24 | 8 | Two checksum words |

The header’s integer fields are stored big-endian. The magic ending in `82` selects little-endian interpretation of words supplied to the checksum algorithm; `83` selects big-endian interpretation. That selection does **not** change the storage byte order of the checksum fields. The four-byte WAL page-size field directly represents the page size, including 65,536 bytes. [SQLite project, *Database File Format*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_write_ahead_log)

| Frame-header offset | Bytes | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| 0 | 4 | Database page number, starting at 1 |
| 4 | 4 | Database size in pages after commit; zero unless this is a commit frame |
| 8 | 8 | Copies of the WAL header’s two salts |
| 16 | 8 | Two cumulative checksum words |
| 24 | Page size | Complete page image |

For page size `P`, one-based frame `i` begins at byte `32 + (i−1) × (24+P)`. Database page numbers identify destinations; frame numbers identify positions in the log. Several frames may therefore identify the same database page. The physical WAL file can also retain obsolete bytes after reuse, so its length does not by itself identify the current committed endpoint. [SQLite project, *Database File Format*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_write_ahead_log)

### Page versions and transaction boundaries

A transaction normally appends page images while leaving their main-database counterparts unchanged. Its final frame carries a nonzero database-size field, making that frame the commit marker. There is no separate commit-record type and no transaction identifier in each frame. Successive commit frames delimit transactions in the valid log sequence.

The commit frame both publishes a transaction boundary and records the resulting logical database size. Frames after the last valid commit can contain a transaction’s unfinished work; their existence, or even valid checksums, does not make that work committed.

A reader captures a committed endpoint when its read transaction begins. For a requested page, it selects the newest applicable frame at or before that endpoint; otherwise it uses the main-database page. Later frames cannot change that reader’s snapshot. This lookup rule works together with checkpoint restrictions: the checkpointer must not overwrite database pages needed by an older reader with versions that reader cannot see. A deferred `BEGIN` alone ordinarily does not establish the snapshot; the first database read does. [SQLite project, *Write-Ahead Logging* and *Isolation in SQLite*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/wal.html) [Isolation details.](https://sqlite.org/isolation.html)

### Checksums and salts serve different purposes

The checksum is cumulative and order-sensitive. Starting with two zero accumulator words, SQLite checksums the first 24 bytes of the WAL header. For each subsequent frame it continues from the preceding checksum state, processing that frame’s first eight header bytes and its complete page image. It excludes the frame’s salts and stored checksum fields from this calculation.

For successive pairs of 32-bit input words, the recurrence is:

```
s0 = s0 + x0 + s1
s1 = s1 + x1 + s0
```

Arithmetic is modulo 2³², and the second line uses the updated `s0`. Because a frame’s checksum incorporates the preceding sequence, recovery validates a log prefix rather than treating frames as independently checksummed records. These checksums detect corruption and incomplete writes; they are not cryptographic authentication. [SQLite project, *Database File Format*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_write_ahead_log)

The salts identify a WAL generation. Every current frame must copy both salts from the current WAL header. On WAL restart, SQLite increments the first salt and selects a new random second salt. This helps distinguish newly written frames from obsolete frames left farther along in a reused file. Salt matching and checksum validation are complementary: matching salts alone do not establish that a frame is valid or committed. [SQLite project, *Database File Format*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_write_ahead_log)

### Recovery and durable commitment

When the WAL index needs rebuilding, SQLite validates the WAL header and scans frames in sequence, checking generation salts and cumulative checksums. An incomplete or invalid frame ends the usable prefix. Within that prefix, the last commit frame determines the recovered committed endpoint and database size; a valid but uncommitted tail is excluded from the recovered database state.

Recovery reconstructs page-to-frame lookup information and coordination metadata. It does not require immediately copying every recovered page into the database file: readers can continue obtaining committed pages from the WAL. The `-shm` file is reconstructible; the WAL can contain committed data absent from the main database and must not be treated as disposable. [SQLite project, *WAL-index File Format* and *Write-Ahead Logging*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/walformat.html) [WAL persistence details.](https://sqlite.org/wal.html)

A commit marker defines a transaction boundary in a valid log, but durability also depends on synchronization and storage behavior. With `synchronous=FULL`, WAL commits synchronize the WAL; with `NORMAL`, most commits omit that synchronization, and recent commits can be lost after a power failure. Transaction visibility, atomic recovery, and persistence across power loss are therefore distinct properties. [SQLite project, *PRAGMA synchronous*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_synchronous)

### Shared-memory WAL index

The WAL index accelerates page lookup and coordinates readers, writers, and checkpoints. With the standard filesystem implementation it is normally mapped through the adjacent `-shm` file. Its representation is machine-dependent and is not the portable, durable database format. Exclusive locking permits WAL operation without a shared-memory file, so the three-file arrangement is the normal case rather than an unconditional requirement. [SQLite project, *Write-Ahead Logging*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/wal.html)

The index uses 32,768-byte regions containing frame-to-page mappings and hash tables for locating candidate frames. A lookup must still choose the newest matching frame no later than the reader’s snapshot boundary; the index is not merely a map to the newest page version globally.

The beginning of the index contains two copies of a 48-byte header. Fields include a change counter, page size, latest committed frame number (`mxFrame`), committed database size, checksum state at that endpoint, and the current salts. Header copies, header checksums, locking, and memory barriers collectively let connections detect and coordinate concurrent updates.

Checkpoint metadata includes `nBackfill`, recording checkpoint progress, and five reader-mark slots. Reader marks are shared coordination slots, **not** a limit of five reader connections: multiple readers can share a suitable slot. A special reader slot supports reading entirely from the main database when the protocol permits it. Writer, checkpoint, recovery, and reader locks occupy designated shared-memory locking locations. These are byte-range locks implemented through SQLite’s VFS, not ordinary persistent lock values written into the WAL. [SQLite project, *WAL-index File Format*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/walformat.html)

### Checkpoint timing and concurrency consequences

A checkpoint copies eligible committed page versions into the main database. It can skip superseded versions rather than replaying every historical frame. SQLite synchronizes the WAL before the relevant database writes, then synchronizes the database before allowing reuse that would discard the WAL’s role in recovery.

By default, a commit that leaves approximately 1,000 or more WAL frames triggers an automatic PASSIVE checkpoint attempt. The threshold is configurable and is a trigger, not a maximum WAL size. Applications can request checkpoints explicitly; SQLite also normally checkpoints during clean shutdown when the last connection closes, subject to configuration and successful completion. [SQLite project, *Write-Ahead Logging*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/wal.html)

PASSIVE checkpoints make available progress without waiting through the busy handler. FULL checkpoints wait as specified by the API to complete backfilling; RESTART additionally waits for readers to release their use of the WAL so a subsequent writer can restart it; TRUNCATE additionally reduces the WAL file to zero bytes. Busy conditions can prevent these requested outcomes. Completing backfill, enabling restart, and truncating the physical file are separate events. [SQLite project, *Checkpoint API*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/c3ref/wal_checkpoint_v2.html)

SQLite permits one writer per database at a time. Readers generally coexist with that writer and retain stable snapshots, but an old reader can constrain checkpoint progress or WAL reuse and allow the WAL to grow. A read transaction that attempts to become a writer after another connection has committed can receive `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT`; it must restart its transaction to write from a current snapshot. WAL therefore supplies snapshot isolation with serialized writers, not unrestricted simultaneous writing or a guarantee that operations never return `SQLITE_BUSY`. [SQLite project, *Isolation in SQLite*, undated.](https://sqlite.org/isolation.html)
